positions.commentary: IBM was a 'granddaddy' of the Nifty 50 that investors couldn't be fired for buying, but it eventually went bankrupt or close to it.
Xerox was the second best company in the Nifty 50 but completely lost its market to imports and had to find a new business model.
Howard Marks states he would have been a disaster investing in Amazon because he is not an optimist, futurist, or financially brave.
The speaker notes that the partner who led the investment in Facebook made a very good decision by letting it ride.
Howard Marks mentions choosing between Merck and Lilly as a task he would avoid doing for the rest of his life.

thesis: This episode argues that investors should hold rare, compounding businesses for decades rather than selling based on price action or short-term concerns, using Amazon and Facebook as primary examples of stocks that rose massively when held through IPOs and long bull runs. It suggests that selling such assets early is a common mistake, and that one should only sell if something extraordinary happens to the company. The thesis also acknowledges that not all investors can replicate these successes, noting that Howard Marks would have been a disaster investing in Amazon due to his lack of optimism and financial bravery.

claims.quote: The granddaddy was IBM, the same way you can't be fired for buying IBM. Did IBM go bankrupt? Maybe, I don't remember, close.

claims.claim: Simplicity Patterns was a consumer company in the Nifty 50 that didn't do well because sewing your own clothes was no longer common.
claims.quote: I'll tell you one consumer company that didn't do well, and that's simplicity patterns. That was in the 50. Do you see a lot of people sewing their own clothes today? If so, you travel in different circles, for me, but that was considered a company that could never be heard.

claims.claim: Xerox was the second best company in the Nifty 50 but completely lost its market to imports and had to find a new business model.
claims.quote: Xerox was number two. They completely lost their market to imports, they had to find a new business model.

claims.claim: The speaker uses Amazon as an example of a stock that rose for 25 years, suggesting one should hold such a chart rather than sell.
claims.quote: If you see a chart of a stock that's been up for 25 years and you say, man, I wish I own that stock, think of all the days you would have had to talk yourself out of selling.

claims.claim: The speaker describes Amazon's rise from 89 in 1999 to 3300, noting that selling early would have been a mistake.
claims.quote: I told the story of Amazon. I think it was 89 in 1999 and then it fell to six in 2001. Let's say you were fortunate enough to buy it at six, would you start selling at 12? Most people would start selling at 12, it's a double. Would you sell at 60?10x? What about 600? 100x? And then it went up to 3300.

claims.claim: The speaker argues that selling Amazon after it went up 100x was a huge mistake because the profit should not be taken off the table.
claims.quote: This idea that as soon as there's a profit, you should take some of it off the table, seems like a huge mistake.

claims.claim: The speaker suggests that selling Amazon based on price action rather than fundamentals is a common mistake.
claims.quote: Most people confuse price action with fundamentals. Oh, this company has been up into the right for years, so it must be a compound or it must be compounding value intrinsically. I think you should make your selling decision based on why you made the investment, how things have evolved, and what you could be playing for.

claims.claim: The speaker notes that if Amazon can compound cash flows for 25 years, it could be up 100x, and holding such a rare company is extremely valuable.
claims.quote: If you really have something that can compound cash flows for 25 years, you're up 100x. If you can do that for 50 years, you're up 10,000x. It's really, really hard to price that in the near term.

claims.claim: The speaker states that if you found something like Amazon, something crazy has to happen for you to sell it.
claims.quote: If you can really believe you found something like that, something crazy has to happen for you to sell it.
